How the forecasts have tested

Each figure is read from the results files of the model version that publishes the number, in tests written down before the data was scored; the earthquake figure is a later second look at its test years, and says so. Ranking accuracy (AUC) is 50% for a coin flip and 100% for a perfect ranking.

Earthquake

96.9%

of the time, a cell that went on to have an M6+ earthquake was ranked above one that did not (a long-term seismicity map alone: 96.7%; difference +0.19 points, 95% interval +0.09 to +0.29)

Every 2° cell, 2023–2025 (a second look at those years)

Hurricane

93%

ranking accuracy of NOAA DTOPS, the probability we publish for the Atlantic, East and Central Pacific; in the same test it beat NOAA SHIPS-RII, NOAA RIOC consensus and our previous model (v8.2). Elsewhere we publish our v8.3 model; it was tested on 2,967 2025–2026 cycles in the basins where it publishes, none used to fit it, 1,078 of them West Pacific

The full track record · How each test was designed

How a forecast is made

  1. Public data in

    Earthquake catalogs from the USGS, tropical cyclone guidance from NOAA’s National Hurricane Center, and NOAA’s live storm tracking and National Weather Service warnings.

  2. A fixed, versioned model

    Each model was chosen by a test written down before the data was scored, and is recorded in the registry with the hash of its file. Changing it means a new version and a new test.

  3. Checked before it is published

    Automatic quality checks run on every forecast: fresh inputs, a valid schema, sane values, a complete record. A failed blocking check stops it.

  4. Frozen, then scored

    Every forecast is saved with its inputs and hashes, chained into a ledger that shows any later edit, and scored against what actually happened.
